questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 5 + 5 + 5?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 5 + 5 + 5 ?
questions.explain: Count the 5s: there are 3 of them, so this is 3 groups of 5, which is 3 × 5 = 15. Counting one group too many gives 4 × 5, which is 5 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 5 × 5 or 4 × 3. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Mei Ling works out 5218 + 2108 in columns. One column makes 16, so she writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.stemText: Mei Ling works out 5218 + 2108 in columns. One column makes 16, so she writes 6 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is that small 1 worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 16 is the ones column: 8 + 8 = 16, and no other column reaches ten. 16 ones is 1 ten and 6 ones, so the 6 stays in the ones column - worth 6 - and the small 1 goes above the tens column - worth 10. The small 1 is worth 10. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.explain: Write down the digits you are told: the tens digit is 3. The ones digit is 2 more than the hundreds digit, so list every pair that works: hundreds 1 and ones 3; hundreds 2 and ones 4; hundreds 3 and ones 5; hundreds 4 and ones 6; hundreds 5 and ones 7; hundreds 6 and ones 8; hundreds 7 and ones 9. questions.explain: The 5 tiles share the 35 cm length equally, so each tile measures 35 ÷ 5 = 7 cm along the row. Its other side is as wide as the whole row: 6 cm. Area of one tile = 7 × 6 = 42 cm². (The whole rectangle is 35 × 6 = 210 cm², and 210 ÷ 5 = 42 cm² too.)

questions.explain: Each square side is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 cm. The 6 squares together: 6 × 4 × 2 = 48 cm. The rectangle: 12 + 2 + 12 + 2 = 28 cm. Difference: 48 − 28 = 20 cm. Shortcut: each of the 5 cuts makes 2 new sides of 2 cm, and 5 × 2 × 2 = 20 cm.

questions.stemText: Kumar has 2 identical rectangular cards. Each card is 14 cm long and 2 cm wide. They are put together, with a long side of one card touching a long side of the other, to make a bigger rectangle. How much shorter is the perimeter of the bigger rectangle than the perimeters of the 2 cards added together?
questions.explain: The 2 cards add up to 2 × (14 + 2 + 14 + 2) = 64 cm. When they touch, the bigger rectangle is 14 cm by 2 + 2 = 4 cm, so its perimeter is 2 × (14 + 4) = 36 cm. Shorter by 64 − 36 = 28 cm: the two touching long sides (14 cm each) are now inside.

questions.stemText: A rectangular banner is 15 cm long and 9 cm wide. A notch 4 cm wide and 2 cm deep is cut out of the middle of one long side, so the notch does not reach either end. Along that side there is 8 cm of edge before the notch and 3 cm after it, and the banner is still 7 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.explain: Walk the eight sides: 8 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 9 + 15 + 9 = 52 cm. Careful: this notch is in the middle of a side, not at a corner. The 4 cm taken out of the top edge is replaced by the 4 cm along the bottom of the notch, so that part of the walk is unchanged. But the two sides of the notch, 2 cm down and 2 cm back up, are brand new. Perimeter = 2 × (15 + 9) + 2 × 2 = 52 cm. A corner cut leaves the perimeter alone; a middle notch makes it longer.
